title: LOVE stamp
lede: The first US Love stamp: an eight-cent issue of 1973 on which Robert Indiana adapted his stacked LOVE image for the United States Postal Service.
summary: Robert Indiana’s stacked LOVE on an eight-cent US postage stamp, 1973.

creator.name: Robert Indiana, for the United States Postal Service

evidence.note: The [National Postal Museum page](https://postalmuseum.si.edu/exhibition/art-of-the-stamp-the-artwork-love/love-1973) and the Smithsonian collection record return HTTP 403 to scripts. The only open image found is a 451 × 287 px copy on [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Lovestamp.png), too small for observation.

styles.note: Pop art’s word-as-image carried into mass print on hundreds of millions of stamps. Partial fit: it has no dots, key lines, or comic devices.

context: In 1973 the United States Postal Service commissioned a stamp design from Indiana and released the eight-cent LOVE stamp before Valentine’s Day. It was unveiled at the Philadelphia Museum of Art, and 425 million were printed over the next two years. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love_(image)).

The image began as a 1964 card that Indiana sent to friends, and in 1965 a red, blue, and green version was chosen for the Museum of Modern Art’s Christmas card. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Love_(image)).
The Commons file gives the issue date as 26 January 1973. [Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Lovestamp.png).
A 1967 screenprint of the same image is [Love](ref:indiana-love-screenprint-1967).
interpretation: The stamp shows how far the Pop idiom travelled into everyday print by the early 1970s: a gallery image reduced to postage size still reads because it is one word in four flat colors.
borrow: Test a Pop headline at icon size: a stacked word in flat color should still read at 40 px.
next: Inspect an image at least 800 px wide, for example through the National Postal Museum in a browser, and add observed traits.

rights.statement: No image is stored. Commons marks its copy public domain with the template PD-textlogo (too simple for copyright), not with a US government or postal rationale, and its source is a cleaned-up web image. The design reproduces Robert Indiana’s LOVE, a privately authored image. The rights need a curator’s decision.
